newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT - Gold price and CRB say inflation no threat.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - Gold price and CRB say inflation no threat.

text.p: The slide in gold prices to three-year lows in January and steady-to-weaker benchmark U.S. commodity price indices during the first month of the year suggest U.S. inflation is likely to remain subdued this year, analysts said.
"If gold is an early warning indicator for inflation, then there is nothing to worry about in 1997," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Edward Yardeni said.
"The spot price of gold has in effect been pegged in a range between $325 and $425 since the late 1980s and it is falling to the bottom of the range, as it did in 1992."
Spot gold in the bullion market was quoted $350.90/351.40 midmorning Wednesday, after sliding to around $347.00 an ounce in mid-January, its lowest levels since September 1993.
"Prospects that a low-inflation environment will support higher equity values suggest that disinvestment of gold will remain in vogue in 1997," Smith Barney analyst David Rinehimer said.
The U.S. Consumer Price Index rose 3.3 percent in 1996, the largest increase since 1996, but was largely driven by higher energy prices.
The core inflation rate, excluding food and energy, was 2.6 percent, the lowest since 1966.
"The gold price is a relatively good leading indicator of PPI (producer price inflation)," Yardeni said.
"The recent decline in the (gold) price suggests that the core PPI inflation rate should remain around zero in 1997."
The December U.S. PPI rose 0.5 percent, for a 2.8 percent year-on-year rise, but excluding food and energy, the PPI rose only 0.1 percent in December and only 0.6 year-on-year.
"Gold price swings also tend to lead movements in bond yields, so the recent drop in gold prices is bullish for bonds," Yardeni said.
The U.S. 30-year treasury bond was trading around 94-21/32 midmorning Wednesday, down from a recent high at 102-27/32 in November 1996, but up from the 1996 lows at 85-18/32 seen in July last year.

But the long term downtrend in gold prices since the early 1980s is partly attributable to selling of gold reserves by central banks in industrial economies, as gold has lost its role in the world's monetary system, analysts noted.

In mid-January the Dutch central bank confirmed it had sold 300 tonnes of gold from its reserves, equivalent to about two-thirds of the annual gold mine output of South Africa, the world's largest gold producer.

Official sector disposals in 1996 are estimated to have been about 300 tonnes, but some analysts suspect official transactions could come to more than 550 tonnes in 1996, up from about 200 tonnes in 1996 and 80 tonnes in 1994.

"We continue to see limited likelihood for a sustained recovery in gold prices without a significant shift in sentiment toward pending selling pressure from central banks, producers and investors," Rinehimer said.
On the charts, spot gold has been in a downtrend for most of the past year, declining from a five-year high at $417 in February 1996.
Spot gold's five-day (weekly) simple moving-average remained below both its 21-day (monthly) average and its 55-day (quarterly) average on Wednesday morning, as it has done for most of the past year.

Weakness in precious metals prices, along with weakness in the energy and tropical products sector, apart from coffee, has offset gains in the grains and base metal sectors in the first few weeks of the new year, leaving benchmark US commodity indices little changed from year-end 1996, analysts said.
The CRB Index was at 241.83 midmorning Wednesday, off its high for 1997 so far at 244.30 on January 16, and little changed from the 239.61 on December 31.
The Goldman Sachs Commodity Index (GSCI), which is more heavily weighted in the energy sector, was at 207.61, down on its December 31 level of 215.26.
"Gold is a very good leading indicator of the CRB futures index and points to a big drop for the index in 1997," Yardeni said.
--Clive McKeef, New York Commodities, +1-212-859-1641.
